label: R8
title: Recitation 8: A Crash Course on Deep Learning
brief: Recitation 8 frames deep learning as the same problem as every lecture, $\min_\theta\frac1n\sum_i\ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i)$, except that $f_\theta$ is a neural network with up to 124 million parameters (a small GPT-2) and the loss is log loss on the next token. The core idea is that deep networks learn their own columns: a hand-made feature such as $x_1^2+x_2^2$ separates two rings perfectly, but with a million pixel columns nobody can design features, so ReLU neurons $h_k=\mathrm{ReLU}(w_k'x+b_k)$ build new columns in which a plane separates the classes, and the nonlinearity is essential because stacked linear layers collapse into one matrix. Such networks are trained by gradient descent with backpropagation, usually as SGD on random batches; different starts reach different minima and there is no optimality certificate. For language, text is split into tokens and each token is looked up as a learned embedding in which cosine similarity and vector arithmetic (king − man + woman ≈ queen) carry meaning, and attention with queries, keys and values updates each vector from the other words, so 'it' attends to 'animal' or 'street' depending on 'tired' or 'wide'. The last vector is scored against all 50,257 tokens and a softmax with temperature $T$ gives next-token probabilities; generation samples, appends and repeats, and because the model predicts likely text it can state false facts. The session closes with research directions from reasoning models and interpretability to scaling laws.
kp: Same objective as the whole course, $\min_\theta\frac1n\sum_i\ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i)$; now $f_\theta$ is a network with up to 124M parameters.
Classical ML needs people to design the columns; deep learning learns them, with linear scores and a softmax on top.
Two rings: logistic regression on $(x_1,x_2)$ gets 51%; adding $x_1^2+x_2^2$ gets 100%; ReLU neurons build such columns automatically.
Without a nonlinearity any stack of linear layers is one matrix, e.g. $W_2(W_1x)=(W_2W_1)x$.
Training is gradient descent with backpropagation, usually SGD on batches; no optimality certificate, different starts give different minima.
Text → tokens (rare words split into pieces) → rows of a learned embedding table; similarity is the cosine of the angle.
Directions encode meaning: king − man + woman → queen.
Attention: $q=W_Qx$, $k=W_Kx$, $v=W_Vx$; queries are matched against keys and values flow to the words that pick them.
Context reaches the query because earlier layers already mixed it into $x$ (the two 'it' vectors: cosine 1.00 at layer 1, 0.90 at layer 7).
A softmax over 50,257 tokens gives next-token probabilities; temperature divides the scores, and models can hallucinate.

topics.x: The optimization problem is unchanged: $\min_\theta\frac1n\sum_i\ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i)$, now with a network, millions of parameters and log loss on the next word. A 1,000×1,000 photo gives a million pixel columns that say little individually, so classical ML relied on experts to design edge, color and texture features. A deep network starts from random weights and fits all layers with one loss; after training, layers contain edge, beak and eye detectors, and reusing one detector at every position gives a CNN.

topics.n: Neurons as new columns, and why nonlinearity
topics.x: On 160 points in two rings, logistic regression on $(x_1,x_2)$ is 51% correct; adding $x_1x_2$ gives 53%, $x_1^2$ 81%, and $x_1^2+x_2^2$ 100%, but that feature engineering works only because we can plot the data. A neuron $h_k=\mathrm{ReLU}(w_k'x+b_k)$ is 0 on one side of its line and grows with distance on the other; in three such columns the inner ring sits near the origin and a plane separates the rings. Without the ReLU, $W_2(W_1x)=(W_2W_1)x$, so any number of linear layers draws the same lines as one.

With 124M parameters and a nonconvex loss we cannot solve to optimality as with MIO. Gradient descent steps $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla L(\theta)$, backpropagation computes all entries of $\nabla L$ with the chain rule, and SGD averages over a random batch (e.g. 512 examples) instead of all $n$ examples. Different starts reach different minima; SGD's noise is a 'drunk walk' that still goes downhill on average and can escape a shallow valley.

Text is split into tokens: common words are one token, rare words several (Bertsimas → Bert|sim|as). One-hot encoding puts every pair of words equally far apart, so each token instead gets a short learned vector (768 numbers) in which similar words cluster. Similarity is the cosine $a'b/(\|a\|\|b\|)$ (BERT: king–queen 0.65, king–man 0.35, king–potato 0.22), and directions encode meaning: king − man + woman → queen, uncle − man + woman → aunt.

The token table gives 'bank' the same vector by a river and in a bank, so each vector must be updated using the other words. Each word's current vector is multiplied by learned matrices to give a query (what it looks for), a key (what it is) and a value (what it passes on): $q=W_Qx$, $k=W_Kx$, $v=W_Vx$. In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired/wide', one BERT head sends 28% of 'it' to 'animal' with tired and 59% to 'street' with wide; the query differs because earlier layers already mixed 'tired' or 'wide' into the 'it' vector.

The last vector scores all 50,257 tokens and a softmax turns the scores into probabilities: 'Paris' gets 6% from GPT-2 (124M) and 69% from GPT-2 medium (355M). Generation samples a token, appends it and repeats; the temperature $T$ divides the scores before the softmax, so $T=0.5$ gives Paris 97% and $T=2$ only 5%. Because the model is trained to predict likely text, it can state false facts, such as crediting the Eiffel Tower to Albert Kahn.

Reasoning models compute longer before answering, trained with rewards on checkable answers; interpretability finds directions that correspond to concepts; agents take actions, with task length doubling about every 7 months (METR). Other directions include efficiency (mixture of experts, distillation, Mamba), diffusion, world models and robots, AI for science (AlphaFold, half of the 2024 Chemistry Nobel) and scaling laws for choosing model size and data under a compute budget.

cards.f: How does the deep-learning training problem differ from earlier lectures?
cards.b: It doesn't in form: $\min_\theta\frac1n\sum_i\ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i)$. Only $f_\theta$ (a network), the size of $\theta$ (124M for a small GPT-2) and $\ell$ (log loss on the next word) change.
cards.x: Same optimization lens, much bigger and nonconvex.

cards.f: Why not hand-design the columns for a bird detector?
cards.b: A 1,000×1,000 photo is a million pixel columns and a single pixel says little; experts used to design edges, colors and textures. Deep learning starts from random weights and learns the columns with one loss.
cards.x: After training, the layers contain edge, beak and eye detectors.

cards.f: Where does the CNN come from in the bird-detector story?
cards.b: Layer 1 needs an edge detector at every position, angle and size; using the same detector at every position gives a convolutional network.
cards.x: Later layers combine edges into beaks and eyes, then heads, then birds.

cards.f: Two-rings data: accuracy by added column?
cards.x: Feature engineering works here only because the data can be plotted.

cards.f: What does a ReLU neuron compute for each point?
cards.b: $h_k=\mathrm{ReLU}(w_k'x+b_k)$: 0 on one side of its line, growing with distance on the other, giving every point a new column.
cards.x: Inner-ring point A maps to (0,0,0); outer points light up at least one neuron.

cards.f: Why does each neuron need a nonlinearity?
cards.b: Linear layers compose into one matrix, $W_2(W_1x)=(W_2W_1)x$, so 100 linear layers draw the same lines as one. ReLU zeroes negative values, so no single matrix reproduces the network.
cards.x: With $W_1,W_2$ from class and $x=(1,-1)$: ReLU network gives $(0,0)$, the linear stack $(-2,0)$.

cards.f: Can we train a 124M-parameter network to optimality?
cards.b: No. The loss is nonconvex; we run gradient descent $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\nabla L(\theta)$ with backprop computing the gradient, different starts reach different minima, and there is no optimality certificate.
cards.x: Contrast with MIO, which proves optimality.

cards.b: GD uses the exact gradient, which averages over all $n$ examples; SGD averages over a random batch (e.g. 512), giving cheaper, noisier steps whose wobbles can carry it out of a shallow valley.
cards.x: Sober hiker vs drunk hiker: both go downhill on average.

cards.f: How is text turned into model input?
cards.b: Split into tokens (common words are one token, rare ones several, e.g. Bertsimas → Bert|sim|as), then look each token up as a row of a learned table.
cards.x: One-hot makes all words equally far apart; embeddings put similar words close.

cards.b: $\cos(a,b)=\frac{a'b}{\|a\|\|b\|}$: 1 for the same direction, 0 for unrelated. BERT: king–queen 0.65, king–man 0.35, king–potato 0.22.
cards.x: Attention uses the same dot product.

cards.f: What does king − man + woman give, and why?
cards.b: The nearest row is queen: the same difference vector (woman − man) maps man to woman and king to queen. Likewise uncle − man + woman → aunt, small − big + bigger → smaller.
cards.x: Directions in embedding space encode meaning.

cards.f: Why isn't one fixed vector per token enough?
cards.b: The table gives 'bank' the same vector in 'grassy bank' and 'deposited cash at the bank'; meaning depends on the other words, so each vector must be updated using them.
cards.x: That update is what attention does.

cards.b: Query: what a word is looking for. Key: what a word says it is. Value: what it passes to words that pick it. Each is the current vector times a learned matrix: $q=W_Qx$, $k=W_Kx$, $v=W_Vx$.
cards.x: A key that fits the query gets a high score.

cards.f: How can 'tired' vs 'wide' change what 'it' attends to if $W_Q$ is fixed?
cards.b: $x_{it}$ differs: earlier layers already mixed 'tired' or 'wide' into it (cosine 1.00 entering layer 1, 0.90 at layer 7), so the query differs; 'animal' gets 28% with tired and 'street' 59% with wide.

cards.f: What does temperature do in generation?
cards.b: It divides the scores before the softmax. Low $T$ concentrates probability on top tokens (Paris 97% at $T=0.5$); high $T$ spreads it (5% at $T=2$); $T=1$ is as trained (69%).
cards.x: Sampling at high $T$ produced 'Augfish seven kilometres outside HEL...'.

cards.b: They are trained to predict likely text, not true facts, so they can state falsehoods: GPT-2 medium said Albert Kahn designed the Eiffel Tower, which Gustave Eiffel's company built.
cards.x: Fluent is not the same as correct.

quiz.q: On the two-rings data, which single added column lets logistic regression reach 100% accuracy?
quiz.e: The rings are circles, so the squared radius separates them perfectly (100%). $x_1^2$ alone reaches only 81%.

quiz.q: A ReLU neuron has $w=(1,2)$ and $b=-1$. What does it output for $x=(1,1)$?
quiz.e: $w'x+b=1+2-1=2>0$, so $\mathrm{ReLU}(2)=2$. 3 forgets the bias; 0 would require a negative input.

quiz.q: Why can't a 124M-parameter network be trained to proven optimality, as with MIO?
o: The loss is nonconvex, so gradient descent gives a solution with no optimality certificate
The data have too few examples
SGD always finds the global minimum, so no certificate is needed
quiz.e: With a nonconvex loss, different starts reach different minima and nothing certifies optimality. Backprop computes the exact gradient by the chain rule; the issue is the landscape.

quiz.q: What is the problem with one-hot encoding words?
o: Every pair of words is equally far apart
It cannot represent rare words at all
It requires a learned matrix per word
quiz.e: One-hot gives one column per word, so 'cat' is as far from 'dog' as from 'car'. Embeddings fix this by giving similar words similar learned vectors.

quiz.q: GPT-2 (124M) gives 'Paris' 6% after 'The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of'. What changes with GPT-2 medium?
o: About 3× the parameters (355M) and Paris rises to 69%
Ten times the parameters and Paris rises to 97%
The same parameters at lower temperature give 69%
About 3× the parameters and Paris falls to 5%
quiz.e: 355M / 124M ≈ 2.9, and the probability of Paris goes from 6% to 69%. 97% and 5% are GPT-2 medium at $T=0.5$ and $T=2$.

quiz.q: Which research direction is described as models that search, run code and call tools, with the task length they complete doubling about every 7 months?
quiz.e: Agents take actions (METR, 2025). Reasoning models compute longer before answering, which is related but not the action-taking direction.

quiz.q: With $W_1=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $W_2=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$, what single matrix equals $W_2(W_1x)$?
quiz.e: $W_2W_1$: row 1 $=(2\cdot1+0\cdot0,\;2\cdot2+0\cdot1)=(2,4)$, row 2 $=(1-0,\;2-1)=(1,1)$. The second option is $W_1W_2$, the wrong order.

o: Every entry of $\nabla L$, all 124M of them, using the chain rule
A certificate that the current minimum is global
quiz.e: Backprop is the chain rule applied systematically to get the full gradient. Choosing a random batch is SGD, a separate idea; no step of training certifies optimality.

quiz.q: Why use SGD instead of exact gradient descent?
o: The exact $\nabla L$ averages over all $n$ examples; a random batch gives much cheaper steps, and its noise can escape shallow valleys
SGD computes a more accurate gradient than full-batch GD
SGD guarantees reaching the deepest valley
SGD removes the need for backpropagation
quiz.e: Each SGD step is cheaper and wobbles because the batch gives a slightly wrong slope; on average it still goes downhill. It is less accurate per step and guarantees nothing about the deepest valley.

quiz.q: What is the cosine similarity of $a=(1,0)$ and $b=(1,1)$?
quiz.e: $a'b=1$, $\|a\|=1$, $\|b\|=\sqrt2$, so $\cos=1/\sqrt2\approx0.71$. 1.41 forgets to divide by $\|b\|$; cosine can never exceed 1.

quiz.q: Using embedding arithmetic, what is the nearest row to small − big + bigger?
quiz.e: bigger − big is the comparative direction; adding it to small gives smaller, just as woman − man added to king gives queen.

quiz.q: In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too wide', where does BERT's attention head send most of 'it'?
quiz.e: A street can be wide, so 'street' gets 0.59 (and 'animal' 0.01). 0.28 to 'animal' is the 'tired' sentence.

quiz.q: $q=W_Qx$ and $W_Q$ is the same in both sentences. How can the query of 'it' depend on 'tired' or 'wide'?
o: Earlier layers already mixed 'tired' or 'wide' into the 'it' vector, so $x_{it}$ differs
The key of 'it' changes, not the query
The token table stores a separate row for each sense of 'it'
quiz.e: Entering layer 1 the two 'it' vectors are identical (cosine 1.00); entering layer 7 they are at 0.90. The matrix is fixed; the input vector carries context.

quiz.q: Lowering the temperature from $T=1$ to $T=0.5$ changes the probability of 'Paris' (GPT-2 medium) how?
o: It stays 69%; temperature only affects sampling speed
quiz.e: Dividing scores by a smaller $T$ widens the gaps between them, concentrating probability on the top token. 5% is $T=2$; 6% to 69% is the model-size change.

quiz.q: An embedding table has one row of 768 numbers for each of 50,257 tokens. How many numbers is that, relative to a 124M-parameter model?
o: About 386M, more than the whole model
quiz.e: $50{,}257\times768\approx38.6$M, and $38.6/124\approx0.31$. 3.9M and 386M are off by a factor of 10.

quiz.q: Two candidate tokens have scores 2 and 0. What is the top token's probability at $T=1$ and at $T=2$?
quiz.e: $T=1$: $e^2/(e^2+1)\approx7.39/8.39\approx0.88$. $T=2$: scores become 1 and 0, so $e/(e+1)\approx0.73$. 0.98 comes from multiplying by $T$ instead of dividing; higher $T$ must spread probability out.

quiz.q: With $W_1,W_2$ from the recitation and a ReLU between the layers, what is the output for $x=(2,-1)$, and what would the purely linear stack give?
quiz.e: $W_1x=(2-2,\,-1)=(0,-1)$, ReLU gives $(0,0)$, and $W_2(0,0)=(0,0)$. Linear: $W_2W_1x=(4-4,\,2-1)=(0,1)$. $(0,-1)$ is only the first layer's pre-activation.

quiz.q: Logistic regression on $(x_1,x_2)$ gets 51% on the rings, yet a plane separates them in the neurons' columns $(h_1,h_2,h_3)$. Why?
o: The ReLU columns map the inner ring near the origin and outer points to large values, so a linear rule in $h$-space is a nonlinear boundary in $x$-space
Three columns always make any two classes linearly separable
The neurons' weights were set by hand to the ring radius
The plane in $h$-space is the same line as in $x$-space
quiz.e: Point A (inner) maps to (0,0,0) while B and C get $h_3=6.2$ and $h_1=5.4$; the network built its own columns, playing the role of the hand-made $x_1^2+x_2^2$. The weights were found by training, and three columns guarantee nothing in general.

written.q: Using the recitation's two-rings example and the bird detector, explain what it means that 'deep learning learns the columns'. Include the role of the nonlinearity (with the $W_1,W_2$ example), how the network is trained, and what guarantees training does and does not give compared with the course's MIO methods.
written.m: Classical ML fits a model such as logistic regression or an optimal tree on columns a person designs. On the two rings, logistic regression on $(x_1,x_2)$ draws a line and gets 51%; adding $x_1x_2$ gives 53%, $x_1^2$ 81%, and $x_1^2+x_2^2$ 100%. That works only because 2-D data can be plotted; a 1,000×1,000 photo has a million pixel columns, none informative alone, so experts historically designed edge, color and texture features. A deep network instead learns the columns: each neuron $h_k=\mathrm{ReLU}(w_k'x+b_k)$ is 0 on one side of a line and grows on the other, so every point gets new columns. In three such columns the inner ring sits near the origin and outer points light up at least one neuron, so a plane separates them, and the final layer is just linear scores plus a softmax. In images, layer 1 learns edge detectors (reused at every position: a CNN), later layers beaks and eyes, then birds. The nonlinearity is essential: $W_2(W_1x)=(W_2W_1)x=\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\1&1\end{bmatrix}x$, so any number of linear layers is one matrix; with a ReLU, $x=(1,-1)$ gives $(0,0)$ instead of $(-2,0)$. Training starts from random weights and minimises one loss by gradient descent, with backpropagation computing all entries of $\nabla L$ and SGD using random batches. Unlike MIO, the loss is nonconvex with up to 124M parameters, different starts reach different minima, and there is no optimality certificate.
k: Neuron as a new column via ReLU; plane separates in $h$-space
Bird detector: edges → parts → birds; CNN reuse
ReLU example breaks the single-matrix equivalence

written.q: Walk through how GPT-2 produces 'Paris' after 'The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of'. Cover tokenization, embeddings and similarity, attention with queries, keys and values (use the 'it' example), the output softmax and temperature, and why the output can be false.
written.m: Tokenization splits the text into tokens: common words are one token, rare words several (Eiffel → E|iff|el). Each token is looked up as a row of a learned table (e.g. 768 numbers); unlike one-hot encoding, where all words are equally far apart, similar words get similar vectors, measured by the cosine $a'b/(\|a\|\|b\|)$ (king–queen 0.65 vs king–potato 0.22), and directions carry meaning (king − man + woman → queen). A fixed row per token cannot handle context ('bank' by a river or with cash), so layers of attention + MLP update each vector using the others. Each word's current vector gives a query $q=W_Qx$ (what it looks for), a key $k=W_Kx$ (what it is) and a value $v=W_Vx$ (what it passes on); keys that fit the query get high scores and their values flow in. In 'the animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired/wide', one head sends 28% of 'it' to 'animal' with tired and 59% to 'street' with wide; $W_Q$ is the same, but earlier layers mixed 'tired' or 'wide' into the 'it' vector (cosine 1.00 at layer 1, 0.90 at layer 7). The last vector scores all 50,257 tokens and a softmax gives probabilities: Paris 6% for the 124M model and 69% for the 355M model. Generation samples a token, appends it and repeats; temperature divides the scores before the softmax (Paris 97% at $T=0.5$, 5% at $T=2$). Because the model is trained to predict likely text, not truth, it can hallucinate, e.g. naming Albert Kahn as the designer when Gustave Eiffel's company built the tower.
k: Q, K, V definitions with $W_Q, W_K, W_V$
'it' example with numbers and the earlier-layer explanation
Temperature divides scores; low concentrates, high spreads
